content: Human parainfluenza virus (HPIV) is an enveloped, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA virus. It is classified into four distinct serotypes: HPIV-1, HPIV-2, HPIV-3, and HPIV-4. The viral genome is approximately 15,000 nucleotides in length and encodes six structural proteins. These proteins are essential for the virus to attach to, enter, and fuse with host cells, forming a complex with the RNA genome. HPIV belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family and is further categorized into one of two genera depending on the serotype: Respirovirus or Rubulavirus. The virus infects the human body by infiltrating white blood cells. Transmission occurs through respiratory droplets in the air or via direct physical contact with an infected individual or contaminated surfaces. The virus utilizes glycoproteins, specifically hemagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion protein, to fuse with white blood cells. Once fusion occurs, the HPIV nucleocapsid is released into the cytoplasm of the host cell. Viral transcription is mediated by a virus-specific RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. The viral mRNAs are subsequently translated into viral proteins, which facilitate the replication of the genome. During replication, the genome is transcribed into both positive-sense RNA strands and negative-sense RNA strands. The negative-sense RNA strand is encapsidated by nucleoprotein and serves as a template for further transcription and replication processes.
